claims.text: What the image looks like Sigmoid wall thickening, pericolonic fat stranding, adjacent diverticula → acute diverticulitis
claims.quote: Sigmoid wall thickening, pericolonic fat stranding, adjacent diverticula Acute diverticulitis

claims.text: Example CT: the colon wall is thickened, with inflammatory streaking (increased density) in the adjacent pericolonic fat
claims.quote: In this axial (cross-sectional) CT image of the abdomen in a person with diverticulitis, the wall of the descending colon is thickened. There is also inflammatory streaking with increased density in the adjacent pericolonic fat.

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) CT of the abdomen and pelvis (oral and rectal water-soluble contrast, plus IV contrast when not contraindicated) is preferred: sensitivity 95 to 99%, specificity 95 to 100%; in about 10% it cannot distinguish diverticulitis from colon cancer
claims.quote: Diverticulitis is evaluated preferentially with CT of the abdomen and pelvis with water-soluble contrast given orally and rectally; IV contrast also is given when not contraindicated (1, 2, 3). CT has a high sensitivity (95 to 99%) and specificity (95 to 100%) for acute diverticulitis (3). However, findings in approximately 10% of patients cannot distinguish diverticulitis from colon cancer.

claims.text: Complicated diverticulitis = abscess, fistula, obstruction or free perforation (about 12% of patients); uncomplicated is the most common
claims.quote: Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis: This is the most common manifestation of acute diverticulitis. Acute complicated diverticulitis: This manifestation is defined by the presence of abscess, fistula, obstruction, or free perforation. Approximately 12% of patients with diverticulitis present with complicated disease (3).

claims.text: MRI is an alternative for pregnant and young patients; ultrasound is another alternative, but accuracy is operator-dependent
claims.quote: MRI is an alternative for pregnant and young patients (4). Ultrasound is another alternative for people with diverticulitis, particularly in the ambulatory setting. Although ultrasound can achieve high accuracy, reported sensitivity (77 to 98%) and specificity (80 to 99%) vary widely and are operator-dependent.

claims.text: Causes Long thought to be a micro or macro perforation of a diverticulum releasing bacteria and triggering inflammation; in some patients it may be more inflammatory than infectious
claims.quote: It has long been thought that diverticulitis occurs when a micro or macro perforation develops in a diverticulum, resulting in the release of intestinal bacteria and triggering inflammation. However, emerging data suggest that in some patients, acute diverticulitis is more of an inflammatory than infectious process.

claims.text: Risk: studies suggest a link with red meat, smoking and obesity; NSAIDs, aspirin, glucocorticoids and opioids increase risk; no association with nuts, seeds, corn or popcorn
claims.quote: Studies have suggested a direct correlation between red meat consumption per week, smoking, obesity, and the incidence of diverticulitis (3, 4). Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), aspirin, glucocorticoids, and opioids also increase the risk of diverticulosis and diverticulitis (3, 4). There is no association between consumption of nuts, seeds, corn, or popcorn and development of diverticulitis as was previously thought (5, 6).

claims.text: Symptoms Left lower quadrant pain and tenderness, often a palpable sigmoid; may come with nausea, vomiting, fever and sometimes urinary symptoms; right-sided disease often gives right-sided pain
claims.quote: Patients have left lower quadrant abdominal pain and tenderness and often have a palpable sigmoid; pain is occasionally suprapubic. However, patients with right-sided diverticulitis often present with right-sided pain. The pain can be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, fever, and sometimes even urinary symptoms as a result of bladder irritation.

claims.text: Peritoneal signs may be present, particularly with abscess or free perforation; fistulas may cause pneumaturia, fecaluria or feculent vaginal discharge
claims.quote: Peritoneal signs (eg, rebound or guarding) may be present, particularly with abscess or free perforation. Fistulas may manifest as pneumaturia, fecaluria (feces in the urine), feculent vaginal discharge, or a cutaneous or myofascial infection of the abdominal wall, perineum, or upper leg.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: outpatient PO antibiotics (uncomplicated); IV abx ± drainage if abscess
claims.quote: Outpatient PO antibiotics (uncomplicated); IV abx ± drainage if abscess

claims.text: Antibiotics may not improve outcomes in uncomplicated diverticulitis: immunocompetent, otherwise healthy patients with uncomplicated sigmoid disease and no significant systemic inflammation or sepsis can often be managed without them; use antibiotics for complicated disease, immunosuppression, sepsis or significant comorbidities
claims.quote: Data suggest that antibiotics may not improve outcomes in uncomplicated diverticulitis; therefore, patients who are immunocompetent, otherwise healthy, and have uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis without evidence of significant systemic inflammation or sepsis can often be safely managed without antibiotics (1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7). Antibiotic therapy should be used for patients with acute complicated diverticulitis, immunosuppression, sepsis, or significant comorbidities.

claims.text: Oral outpatient options (7 to 10 days) include metronidazole plus a fluoroquinolone, metronidazole plus a cephalosporin, metronidazole plus TMP/SMX, or amoxicillin/clavulanate
claims.quote: Oral antibiotic regimens that can be given to outpatients for whom treatment is elected include 7 to 10 days of one of the following (3, 8): Metronidazole plus a fluoroquinolone (eg, ciprofloxacin) Metronidazole plus a cephalosporin (eg, cephalexin) Metronidazole plus trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole Amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid

claims.text: CT-guided percutaneous or EUS-guided drainage for larger abscesses (over 3 to 4 cm), abscesses not resolving with antibiotics, or deterioration
claims.quote: CT-guided percutaneous or endoscopic ultrasound-guided drainage is becoming the standard of care for larger abscesses (over 3 to 4 cm in diameter), for abscesses that do not resolve with antibiotics, and/or for clinical deterioration (1, 6).

claims.text: Immediate surgery for free perforation or suspected feculent peritonitis
claims.quote: Surgery is required immediately for patients with free perforation or when feculent peritonitis is suspected based on clinical examination or imaging (1).

claims.text: Colonoscopy 6 to 8 weeks after complicated diverticulitis, and after uncomplicated disease with alarm symptoms or if not current with colon cancer screening
claims.quote: Colonoscopy is recommended 6 to 8 weeks after an episode of complicated diverticulitis and for patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis if they have alarm symptoms or if they are not current with colon cancer screening (7, 9, 10).
